content.title: About
content.content: Apricot nectar is a sweet beverage made from ripe apricots, water and a small amount of sugar. Apricots (Prunus armeniaca) originate from Central Asia but are now cultivated in many warm regions worldwide. The nectar retains the fruit’s characteristic aroma and a light tang, while providing the vitamins and minerals typical of fresh apricots.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Apricots belong to the Rosaceae family and are closely related to peaches, plums and cherries.
Traditional nectar is produced by heating apricot puree with water and sugar, then straining the mixture.
In several countries apricot nectar is a classic summer refresher.
It contains more vitamin A than most other fruit drinks.
Apricot nectar is often used in sauces, desserts and cocktails.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function and skin health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts antioxidant protection and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes normal digestion and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The nectar contains virtually no fat, making it a light beverage.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugar means people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Apricot allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to apricots.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach in people with gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve apricot nectar chilled as a standalone drink, use it in cocktails, smoothies, desserts, or as a sauce for meat and fish. It can also be added to tea or yogurt for a fruity flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: After opening, keep the nectar refrigerated in a tightly sealed bottle and consume within 5–7 days. Unopened product should be stored in a cool, dry place at up to 20 °C; see the package for the best‑before date.

fish-shish-kabob-with-vegetables-excludi.title: Fish Shish Kabob with Vegetables (No Potatoes)

content.title: About
content.content: Fish shish kabob with vegetables is a dish where chunks of fish (commonly salmon or cod) are threaded onto skewers together with a mix of vegetables (bell pepper, zucchini, onion, cherry tomatoes) and grilled or baked. Potatoes are omitted, making the meal lighter and lower in carbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fish kebabs are a staple in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines.
The vegetables used are rich in antioxidants that help protect cells from oxidative stress.
Grilling preserves most of the omega‑3 fatty acids in the fish.
The recipe can be adapted for dietary needs by swapping fish for seafood or tofu.
Excluding potatoes lowers the glycemic index of the dish, beneficial for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Fish, especially salmon and mackerel, provides EPA and DHA – fatty acids that support heart and brain health.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: A serving delivers about 20‑25 g of protein, essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fish and vegetables supply B12, B6, and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains selenium, iodine, magnesium, and potassium, which aid thyroid function and nerve health.

items.title: Vegetable antioxidants
items.content: Bell peppers and tomatoes are high in vitamin C and lycopene, helping combat free radicals.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Certain fish can contain mercury or cadmium; choose reputable sources and limit intake to 2‑3 servings per week.

items.title: Over‑cooking
items.content: Excessive charring can create acrylamide in vegetables; aim for a golden brown, not blackened, finish.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the kabob hot, straight from the grill, with a squeeze of lemon, a yogurt‑herb sauce, or fresh parsley. It pairs well with a side salad, cauliflower rice, or whole‑grain couscous.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in the oven or on a skillet rather than the microwave to retain texture.

content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger on a white bun with one large patty (1707) is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a soft bun, a juicy beef patty, lettuce, tomato slice, onion, cheese and sauce of choice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hamburger was served in the United States in the late 19th century.
The name comes from the German port of Hamburg, where the “Hamburg steak” originated.
McDonald’s popularized the hamburger worldwide in the 1960s.
There are over 100 hamburger variations, including vegetarian and gluten‑free versions.
The world’s largest burger patty weighed more than 200 kg.

items.title: Protein
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Red meat is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburgers contain vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Energy
items.content: Carbohydrates from the bun and fats from the meat and cheese quickly replenish energy stores.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauces and cheese often contain a lot of salt, which can affect blood pressure.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A single hamburger can contain 400–800 kcal, important to consider in a diet.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Cheese, bread and sauces may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Meat safety
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can lead to foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten with the hands, holding the bun. Additional vegetables, sauces, or alternative patties (chicken, turkey, plant‑based) can be added to suit taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A prepared hamburger is best consumed immediately. If needed, store it in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Frozen patties keep for up to 3 months, and buns for up to 2 weeks.

content.title: About
content.content: Kung Pao Chicken is a classic Chinese dish featuring diced chicken breast stir‑fried with peanuts, dried chilies, vegetables, and a savory soy‑based sauce. It delivers a spicy‑sweet flavor profile and the distinctive aroma of Sichuan peppercorns.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in Sichuan province in the 19th century and was originally made with duck.
The name “Kung Pao” (宫保) comes from the title “Gongbao,” held by the Qing‑dynasty official Ding Baozhen.
Traditional recipes use dried red chilies, but the heat level can be adjusted to taste.
Peanuts add a crunchy contrast to the tender chicken pieces.
The classic sauce combines soy sauce, rice vinegar, and sugar for a balanced sweet‑savory taste.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides a complete source of high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Peanuts supply monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish offers niacin, vitamin B6, and other B‑vitamins that aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Dried chilies and soy sauce contain antioxidants that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium, and zinc are present, contributing to immune function and metabolic processes.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce adds significant salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Spiciness of chilies
items.content: Dried chilies may irritate the gastrointestinal tract; those with sensitive stomachs should reduce the amount.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑rich due to oil and nuts; moderation is advised for weight‑controlled diets.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Kung Pao Chicken is typically served hot with steamed rice or noodles. Garnish with fresh cilantro or sliced green onions and sprinkle extra peanuts for added crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat with a splash of oil to retain the peanuts’ crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: The Multiple Meat Sandwich on Wheat (1857) is a hearty sandwich made with slices of beef, chicken and ham layered between two pieces of whole‑grain wheat bread. It provides protein, iron and B‑vitamins, as well as fiber from the whole grain.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The recipe combines three types of meat, enhancing flavor complexity and nutritional value.
Wheat bread supplies slow‑release energy thanks to its complex carbohydrates.
This sandwich is a common offering in school cafeterias and at sporting events as a quick energy source.
Meat can be lightly pan‑seared to retain juiciness and aroma.
Some versions add fresh vegetables—tomato, lettuce, cucumber—for extra vitamins.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Three meat varieties deliver a high amount of complete protein essential for muscle repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole‑grain bread contain B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Wheat bread adds dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and complex carbs helps maintain fullness longer.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergies or intolerances to specific meats.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: If the meat is pre‑salted or smoked, sodium levels can be high, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be enjoyed cold or gently warmed in a microwave. Cut it in half for children, add fresh veggies, mustard, or a light yogurt sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, keep the meat and bread separate: meat in the fridge, bread in a dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: Yokan is a traditional Japanese jelly‑like dessert made from agar‑agar, sugar and sweet red bean paste (anko). It has a firm, slightly springy texture and a mild sweetness, usually served in small cubes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yokan originated in Japan during the Edo period and was originally a treat for the aristocracy.
Traditional yokan uses red bean paste, but there are variations with green tea, pumpkin, and black sesame.
The agar‑agar used in yokan is derived from seaweed, making the dessert vegan.
Yokan is often packaged in lacquered boxes as a gift.
In Japan yokan is commonly enjoyed with green tea, as its sweetness balances the tea’s bitterness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Yokan contains virtually no fat, making it a light dessert option.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Red bean paste provides a modest amount of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Red beans are a good source of dietary fiber, supporting digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in the beans help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten‑ and lactose‑free
items.content: Yokan is suitable for people with gluten or lactose intolerance.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to red beans.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional yokan is sweetened, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Agar‑agar sensitivity
items.content: Large amounts of agar‑agar can cause mild digestive upset in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Yokan is typically cut into small cubes and served as a light dessert after a meal. It can be eaten on its own, paired with tea, or used as a filling for sweet rolls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store yokan in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze it in a tightly sealed bag and thaw at room temperature before serving.
